{{Short description|Theorem in classical algebraic geometry}}
In classical [[algebraic geometry]], the '''genus–degree formula''' relates the degree <math>d</math> of an [[Irreducible polynomial|irreducible]] [[plane curve]] <math>C</math> with its [[arithmetic genus]] <math>g</math> via the formula:
:<math>g=\frac12 (d-1)(d-2).</math>
Here "plane curve" means that <math>C</math> is a closed curve in the [[projective plane]] <math>\mathbb{P}^2</math>. If the curve is non-singular, then the [[geometric genus]] and the [[arithmetic genus]] are equal, but if the curve is singular, with only ordinary singularities, then the geometric genus is smaller. More precisely, an ordinary [[Mathematical singularity|singularity]] of multiplicity <math>r</math> decreases the genus by <math>\frac12 r(r-1)</math>.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Semple|authorlink1=John Greenlees Semple| first1=John Greenlees|last2= Roth|first2=Leonard | authorlink2=Leonard Roth| title=Introduction to Algebraic Geometry|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |edition= 1985 |mr=0814690 |isbn=0-19-853363-2|pages= 53–54}}</ref>

== Motivation ==
[[Elliptic curve]]s are parametrized by [[Weierstrass elliptic function]]s. Since these parameterizing functions are doubly periodic, the elliptic curve can be identified with a period parallelogram with the sides glued together ''i.e.'' a torus. So the genus of an elliptic curve is 1. The genus–degree formula is a generalization of this fact to higher genus curves. The basic idea would be to use higher degree equations. Consider the quartic equation<math display="block">\left(y^2-x(x-1)(x-2)\right)\,(5 y-x)+\epsilon x=0.</math>For small nonzero <math>\varepsilon</math> this is gives the nonsingular curve. However, when <math>\varepsilon=0</math>, this is<math display="block">\left(y^2-x(x-1)(x-2)\right)\,(5 y-x)=0,</math>a reducible curve (the union of a nonsingular cubic and a line). When the points of infinity are added, we get a line meeting the cubic in 3 points. The complex picture of this reducible curve looks like a torus and a sphere touching at 3 points. As <math>\varphi</math> changes to nonzero values, the points of contact open up into tubes connecting the torus and sphere, adding 2 handles to the torus, resulting in a genus 3 curve.

In general, if <math>g(d)</math> is the genus of a curve of degree <math>d</math> nonsingular curve, then proceeding as above, we obtain a nonsingular curve of degree <math>d+1</math> by <math>\varepsilon</math>-smoothing the union of a curve of degree <math>d</math> and a line. The line meets the degree <math>d</math> curve in <math>d</math> points, so this leads to the recursion<math display="block">g(d+1)=g(d)+d-1,\quad g(1)=0.</math>This recursion has the solution <math>g(d)=\frac12(d-1)(d-2)</math>.

== Proof ==
The genus–degree formula can be proved from the [[adjunction formula]]; for details, see {{slink|Adjunction formula|Applications to curves}}.<ref>''Algebraic geometry'', [[Robin Hartshorne]], Springer GTM 52, {{ISBN|0-387-90244-9}}, chapter V, example 1.5.1</ref>

== Generalization ==
For a non-singular [[hypersurface]] <math>H</math> of degree <math>d</math> in the [[projective space]] <math>\mathbb{P}^n</math> of [[arithmetic genus]] <math>g</math> the formula becomes:

: <math>g=\binom{d-1}{n} , \,</math>

where <math>\tbinom{d-1}{n}</math> is the [[binomial coefficient]].
